title: Foundations of Nursing Practice: Oxygenation Basics & Respiratory Safety
html:
Oxygenation is a basic physiologic need and a priority when breathing changes. The RN combines what the client reports, direct observation, vital signs, pulse oximetry, and the response to treatment. A number on a monitor never replaces assessment of airway, breathing effort, mental status, and overall appearance.

Learning goals

  • Perform a focused respiratory assessment and recognize worsening work of breathing.
  • Interpret pulse oximetry as one data point in the clinical picture.
  • Apply prescribed oxygen safely and check equipment systematically.
  • Identify cues that require immediate respiratory escalation.
  • Evaluate the client's response rather than assuming a device is working.

Assess breathing before the monitor

Ask about shortness of breath, cough, sputum, chest discomfort, onset, triggers, respiratory history, medications, and baseline function. Observe level of consciousness, respiratory rate over a full minute, rate, rhythm, depth, chest expansion, skin and mucous-membrane color, ability to speak, and use of accessory muscles. Restlessness, anxiety, confusion, nasal flaring, retractions, audible breathing, cyanosis, or a marked change from baseline can signal respiratory difficulty.

Start with ABCs
Sudden inability to speak, stridor, cyanosis, severely increased work of breathing, declining consciousness, or acute respiratory distress requires an immediate emergency response. Do not delay for a complete history or a repeat routine vital-sign set.

Use pulse oximetry wisely

SpO2 is an estimate of hemoglobin saturation, not a complete picture of ventilation or tissue oxygen delivery. Compare the reading with the client's prescribed target or baseline and assess the waveform or signal quality when available. Poor peripheral perfusion, motion, sensor placement, nail products, and other factors can make a reading misleading. When a reading is unexpected, first assess the client and sensor, obtain the required repeat measurement, and escalate according to the condition and policy.

Do not use a normal-looking SpO2 value to dismiss visible respiratory distress, and do not change a prescribed oxygen setting solely to chase a number. Some clients have individualized targets, so the order and care plan guide management.

Administer oxygen safely

Supplemental oxygen is a treatment that is prescribed and monitored, except where an emergency protocol authorizes immediate action. Verify the client, order, prescribed device, flow or concentration, target if stated, and current assessment. Check that the equipment is connected correctly, tubing is not kinked, and the device fits without causing pressure injury. Keep oxygen away from flames, sparks, smoking materials, and other ignition sources. Use only approved products and follow the facility process for humidification, transport, portable cylinders, and device care.

Do not independently substitute a device, adjust flow, or stop therapy because the client appears better. If the client deteriorates, start with airway and breathing assessment, obtain help, and act under the emergency process and scope of practice.

Recognize and communicate a change

Describe what is observed: “respiratory rate 30, speaking in short phrases, new accessory-muscle use, SpO2 below prescribed target despite ordered oxygen” communicates risk more clearly than “breathing looks bad.” Reassess after positioning or any intervention, compare with baseline, and report the trend using the team's escalation framework. The cause may be pulmonary, cardiac, neurologic, medication-related, or otherwise; the RN recognizes and communicates cues without prematurely naming a diagnosis.

Evaluate the response

After an intervention, reassess work of breathing, ability to speak, respiratory rate and pattern, lung findings as appropriate, mental status, skin color, pulse oximetry in context, comfort, and device tolerance. Verify that equipment still delivers the ordered treatment. Improvement or deterioration guides the next action and documentation.

Clinical example

An RN enters a room and finds a client sitting forward, speaking only two-word phrases, with new accessory-muscle use. Although the pulse-oximeter sensor displays a value close to the prior reading, the RN assesses ABCs, activates the appropriate urgent response, checks the ordered oxygen system, and reassesses while help arrives. The visible deterioration matters more than waiting for a perfect number.
